abstract: Visual working memory tasks rely on neural systems that scale activity with task load. Traditional models assume higher demands are met by monotonically increasing activity within a single process, implying high informational redundancy across responses. However, theories of cognitive control suggest processing strategies change with task demands, flexibly linking sensory inputs to behavior. Using 7T fMRI and neural encoding models, we hypothesized and confirmed that association cortices format task load-dependent responses using sensory-like neural tuning. We identified populations selectively tuned to specific loads, forming 11 topographic maps per hemisphere hierarchically organized from posterior sensory to anterior executive regions across a fronto-parieto-occipital network. Tuning persisted across performance and trial-order controls, was absent without memory task demands, and predicted behavioral accuracy after load changes. These findings demonstrate that human association cortices distribute task demands using continuously varying processing pathways, adapting sensory-like tuning to decorrelate responses and reduce information redundency during cognitive control.
